title: A Comparative Study of Technical Writing Feedback Quality: Evaluating LLMs, SLMs, and Humans in Computer Science Topics
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students perceive the quality of technical-writing feedback generated by large language models (LLMs), small language models (SLMs), and humans in computing education. The core questions are whether students view AI-generated feedback as higher or lower quality than human feedback, whether they can distinguish AI from human feedback, and whether AI systems can support scalable feedback processes more efficiently than instructors or teaching assistants.

The intervention was a feedback-generation system using GPT-4 as the LLM and Meta LLaMA 3.1 8B as the SLM, supported by retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over course materials, rubrics, and assignment documents. Students in three undergraduate computer science-related courses viewed three anonymized feedback versions on their own submitted work—LLM, SLM, and human—and then rated them on readability, detail, specificity, actionability, helpfulness, and overall quality, while also providing qualitative comments. The study combined Likert-scale survey data with thematic analysis of open-ended responses.

The population consisted of undergraduate students at a single North American research-focused institution in Canada, across an introductory computer science course, an upper-year operating systems course, and a small upper-year writing course on AI topics. Valid survey responses included 176 students in CS2, 80 in operating systems, and 7 in the writing course. Human feedback came from teaching assistants in some courses and the course instructor in the writing course.

The main conclusions are that AI-generated feedback, especially from the SLM, was often perceived as clear, structured, and actionable in large technical courses, while human feedback was preferred when assignments required personalized, context-sensitive, and nuanced guidance. In the small writing-intensive course, all respondents preferred instructor feedback. Students could often, but not always, identify whether feedback came from AI or humans. The authors argue that AI feedback is promising for scalability and efficiency, but that hybrid human-in-the-loop models are likely the most pedagogically effective approach.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods comparative study with quantitative survey data and some statistical testing, but it is not a K-12 study, lacks random assignment, and focuses on student perceptions of feedback rather than direct learning outcomes. It appears to be an arXiv preprint/grey literature source with limited causal credibility for the requested K-12 evidence framework.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but context-dependent perceived benefits of AI feedback, especially for efficiency and some feedback-quality dimensions, but impact on actual writing achievement is unclear and no standardized effect sizes are reported. Results are mixed across contexts, with human feedback preferred in the small writing-intensive course.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI-based automated feedback on students’ technical writing submissions in computer science courses, comparing GPT-4 and LLaMA 3.1 8B with human TA/instructor feedback using a rubric-aligned prompt and retrieval-augmented generation.
LLM/SLM writing-feedback tool for technical documentation and report-writing, generating criterion-by-criterion comments, reasoning, and revision suggestions for student writing.

finding.finding_summary: The study examined perceived quality of feedback on student technical writing rather than objective writing achievement. In the operating systems course (n=80 valid responses), students most often preferred SLM feedback (61.25%) over LLM (15%) and human (23.75%), with statistically significant advantages for SLM on readability (p=0.005), actionability (p=0.040), and overall quality (p=0.004), while in the small writing course (n=7) all students preferred instructor feedback across all writing-feedback dimensions. In the CS2 course (n=176 valid responses), humans had the best readability mean (1.83), but SLM feedback was rated more favorably on most other feedback dimensions; no standardized effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student ratings of feedback quality for technical writing (readability, detail, specificity, actionability, helpfulness, overall quality), plus feedback preference selections

finding.finding_summary: AI-supported feedback generation substantially reduced time demands relative to human marking. For the operating systems course (143 enrolled students), humans reportedly spent about 35 hours writing feedback plus 5 hours training, whereas the SLM system generated all feedback in about 1.8 hours; for the 13-student writing course, SLM generation took about 10 minutes versus about 4.5 hours of instructor marking, and GPT-4 averaged roughly 25 seconds per response. These findings suggest strong efficiency gains, though they are descriptive and not tied to randomized productivity comparisons.
finding.measure: Time to generate feedback, estimated staffing time/cost, scalability of feedback delivery

finding.finding_summary: The paper indirectly assessed students’ ability to evaluate and discern feedback sources, which relates to judgment and critical evaluation rather than direct academic performance. Students identified feedback origin with 100% accuracy in the small writing course, 69.58% overall accuracy in operating systems, and lower accuracy in CS2 for LLM (34.66%) and SLM (52.84%) identification, suggesting variable student capacity to critically distinguish AI from human feedback depending on context. No validated durable-skills measure or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy in identifying whether feedback was AI- or human-generated
